newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean memory chip exports seen slowing further.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean memory chip exports seen slowing further.

text.p: South Korea's chipmaking industry is expected to suffer for another year from sagging world memory chip prices due to a persistent global oversupply, analysts said on Wednesday.
But the emergence of a 64-megabit DRAM chip market in 1998 was seen helping the battered industry recover from its two-year slump, they added.
The Korea Semiconductor Industry Association forecast this year's semiconductor exports -- excluding the assembly sector -- at $10 billion, down from an estimated $11 billion in 1996.

Memory chip exports, which make up the majority of South Korea's semiconductor exports, were forecast to fall 10.2 percent to $8.8 billion in 1997 from an estimated $9.8 billion in 1996, the association said.
"Memory chip prices will continue to drop this year, although the pace will be much slower than last year," said Tony Jung, an analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities in Seoul.

The association saw the price of the most widely used 16-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chip falling to $6 per unit. In 1996, prices plunged to $8 in the fourth quarter from around $34 in the first quarter.

The fall in chip prices was blamed for the surge in the country's trade deficit in 1996, when South Korean exporters saw their competitiveness challenged by both cheap labour-backed developing economies and advanced nations.

South Korea's trade deficit ballooned to a record $20.38 billion in 1996 from a $10.06 billion shortfall in 1995, while semiconductor exports fell 19.2 percent to $17.87 billion in 1996 from $22.1 billion in 1995.
The slump in memory chip exports has led to a plunge in the earnings of South Korea's major chipmakers, which are heavily concentrated on DRAM sales.
Analysts estimate after-tax net profit of Samsung Electronics Co at around 300 billion won ($352 million) in 1996, less than one-eighth of last year's net earnings of 2.5 trillion won.
A spokeswoman for Samsung, one of the world's largest DRAM suppliers, said its 1996 earnings figures were not yet finalised, but said DRAM sales had been seriously damaged by weak prices.
"We have no official figures yet, but our DRAM sales in 1996 will be close to $6.5 billion, compared with around $8.3 billion in 1995," said Lee Eun-kyung.

Jung of Jardine Fleming saw Samsung's net profit further deteriorating in 1997 while profits of the other two of South Korea's top three chipmakers were expected to rebound as recent capacity expansion began paying off.
He forecast net profit of Hyundai Electronics Industries Co and LG Semicon Co Ltd would each rise to around 65 billion won in 1997 from an estimated 50 billion won in 1996.

But a turnaround would come when a wider market emerged for 64-megabit DRAM chips in 1998, boosted by rising demand for multimedia software requiring stronger capacity, analysts said. (US$1 = 852 won)
